Model comparison findings¶

  • Selected Ridge specification: 2023 tuning selected the 20-feature model containing K% history, workload and availability, Stuff+, and centered age terms, with $\alpha=0.1$. Adding two league-context features improved MAE by less than the prespecified 0.01-percentage-point threshold, so the parsimony rule favored the simpler model.
  • Out-of-time 2024 result: Ridge produced a 5.26-percentage-point MAE and 7.26-point RMSE, compared with Marcel's 5.86-point MAE and 8.38-point RMSE. Thus, the fitted model improved both primary metrics in the season that was not used for feature or penalty selection.
  • Combined 2023–2024 result: Ridge reduced unweighted MAE from 5.85 to 5.31 percentage points, an improvement of 0.54 points. Gradient boosting reached 5.46 points and did not justify its added complexity. OLS nearly matched Ridge, but Ridge is preferred because coefficient shrinkage provides protection against the substantial overlap among the historical-rate features.
  • Same-sample prior-year comparison: across the same 1,718 validation pitcher-seasons, prior-season K% produced a 6.17-point MAE versus Ridge's 5.31 points. Ridge therefore improved MAE by 0.85 percentage points without benefiting from an easier evaluation sample.
  • Visual diagnostics: individual actual K% values are much more dispersed than Ridge predictions, especially for small workloads; this is the expected effect of regression toward the mean. The calibration deciles follow the 45-degree line reasonably closely. Ridge mildly underpredicted several middle bins and mildly overpredicted the lowest and highest bins, but the average gaps were small relative to individual-season noise.
  • Important weighting tradeoff: Marcel retained the better TBF-weighted MAE, 3.33 versus 3.60 percentage points. Ridge's advantage was concentrated among difficult low-information players: for players with 1–49 prior TBF, Ridge reduced unweighted MAE from 8.38 to 5.66 points. Marcel remained slightly better for players with at least 200 prior TBF, 3.35 versus 3.40 points. Limited or incomplete prior history represented 1,065 of 1,718 validation pitcher-seasons (62%), versus 653 (38%) with at least 200 prior TBF. Low TBF should not be equated automatically with relief pitching; it can also reflect injury, a midseason debut, or occasional position-player pitching.
  • Why not switch models at a TBF cutoff? A segmented model is valid in principle, but choosing a cutoff from the combined 2023–2024 results and reporting performance on those same seasons would overfit the validation evidence. The 50–199 TBF group was essentially tied and Marcel's 200+ advantage was only 0.05 percentage points of unweighted MAE. Ridge also already receives Marcel K%, Marcel reliability, and workload features, allowing it to use that information continuously. With only two validation seasons, the small possible gain did not justify a new hard rule.
  • Feature interpretation: Stuff+ and age improved the 2023 selection result, and the 2024 feature-set comparison remained close. Individual coefficients should not be interpreted causally or in isolation because several predictors describe overlapping aspects of the same pitching history.

How Marcel is used: Marcel serves two roles: it is evaluated as a standalone benchmark, and its projected K% and reliability are also supplied as features to Ridge. The final prediction is produced by Ridge, which learns how much Marcel information to use alongside the other features.

Model decision: use Ridge for the 2025 case-study projections because unweighted MAE matches the one-prediction-per-player objective. Retain Marcel as a transparent benchmark and document that it would be preferred if high-workload accuracy were the primary objective. A pre-2025 swinging-strike metric remains a possible challenger rather than an assumed improvement. The 2025 outcomes remain sealed.

Role scope control: starter/reliever role was considered because role can affect strikeout rates, but the dataset does not include games started, appearances, or innings. TBF alone cannot reliably distinguish relievers from starters, injured pitchers, or midseason call-ups, and actual 2025 roles would not be permissible pre-season information. Rather than introduce a potentially misleading classification, the model retains workload and history indicators; a future extension could construct prior-season role from pre-2025 GS/G and innings data, with a separate mixed-role category.

Final 2025 predictions¶

The model specification is now frozen: Ridge with the feature set and penalty selected using the historical process above. The final model is refit on all 2,589 eligible 2022–2024 target player-seasons, allowing the imputer, scaler, and Ridge coefficients to learn from every permissible training example. It then scores the 873-player 2025 feature table built only from performance through 2024 and target-season age.

Refitting after model selection is standard because the 2024 outcomes can improve the final coefficient estimates once they are no longer being used to choose among specifications. No 2025 K%, TBF, Stuff+, or team information enters the model. The exported K% values use the same decimal scale as the source file: for example, 0.250000 means 25.00%.

# Development assistance: OpenAI Codex supported code structure and review.
# https://openai.com/codex/

# Refit the frozen Ridge specification on every permissible target season.
final_ridge_model = make_linear_pipeline(Ridge(alpha=BEST_RIDGE_ALPHA))
final_ridge_model.fit(baseline_backtest[SELECTED_FEATURES], baseline_backtest["K%"])

raw_2025_prediction = final_ridge_model.predict(features_2025[SELECTED_FEATURES])
final_2025_prediction = np.clip(raw_2025_prediction, 0.0, 1.0)

# Preserve the source player order and express K% on the source decimal scale.
predictions_2025 = features_2025[["PlayerId", "Name"]].copy()
predictions_2025.insert(0, "Season", 2025)
predictions_2025["Predicted K%"] = final_2025_prediction

# Final integrity checks prevent missing, duplicate, or illogical projections.
assert len(predictions_2025) == len(players_2025)
assert predictions_2025["PlayerId"].is_unique
assert set(predictions_2025["PlayerId"]) == set(players_2025["PlayerId"])
assert predictions_2025["Predicted K%"].notna().all()
assert predictions_2025["Predicted K%"].between(0.0, 1.0).all()

output_dir = project_root / "outputs"
output_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
prediction_output_path = output_dir / "k_2025_predictions.csv"
predictions_2025.to_csv(prediction_output_path, index=False, float_format="%.6f")

projection_audit = pd.Series({
    "training_player_seasons": len(baseline_backtest),
    "projected_players": len(predictions_2025),
    "minimum_prediction_pct": predictions_2025["Predicted K%"].min() * 100,
    "median_prediction_pct": predictions_2025["Predicted K%"].median() * 100,
    "maximum_prediction_pct": predictions_2025["Predicted K%"].max() * 100,
    "clipped_predictions": int((raw_2025_prediction != final_2025_prediction).sum()),
})
display(projection_audit.to_frame("value").round(2))
print(f"Saved final predictions to: {prediction_output_path.relative_to(project_root)}")

Final projection graphics¶

The distribution chart is a final plausibility check. It shows the spread of all 873 projections and compares the unweighted 2025 projection median with the comparable unweighted 2024 player-season median. The projection distribution should be narrower than the distribution of observed single-season K% because the model deliberately regresses noisy and limited histories toward typical values. The TBF-weighted 2024 league K% is not used as the chart reference because it answers a different question by giving established, high-workload pitchers much more influence.

The top-20 chart translates the model into an intuitive baseball result. It ranks projected K% only, not overall pitcher quality, expected workload, or total strikeouts. Bar colors show how much immediately prior history is available; this is important because a high-rate forecast for a pitcher with limited or missing 2024 history carries more uncertainty than the same forecast for an established pitcher.

Limitations and possible improvements¶

  1. Short validation history. The dataset begins in 2021, leaving 2023 for specification selection and only 2024 as the untouched final validation season. Results from two forecast years may not generalize perfectly across run environments or changes in league strategy.
  2. Truncated pitcher histories. Available-history features summarize only the recorded seasons before each target year, not a pitcher's complete MLB career. Earlier MLB performance, minor-league data, injuries, and offseason changes are unavailable. This is especially important for pitchers with no or little recorded history.
  3. Role and context are not modeled directly. TBF is not synonymous with starter or reliever status. The model does not explicitly know future role, expected workload, handedness, pitch mix, velocity, team defense, park, catcher, or opponent quality. Target-season TBF cannot be known at projection time.
  4. Position-player pitching complicates league regression. Regressing a small or missing sample toward league-average pitcher K% assumes that the player belongs to the pitcher population. That is reasonable for an inexperienced pitcher but can overproject a position player making emergency appearances. Ridge can partially learn from low workload, missingness, prior K%, and Stuff+, but it cannot reliably distinguish a rookie pitcher from a position player when neither has supplied pitching history. A future model could add a primary-position indicator known before 2025 and estimate a separate position-player pitching baseline.
  5. The evaluation objective matters. Ridge leads on equal-player MAE, while Marcel leads on TBF-weighted MAE. A high-workload-focused application could rationally prefer Marcel. A TBF-gated blend was not adopted because the apparent cutoff advantage was small, the 50–199 TBF group was tied, and the short validation window could make a post hoc cutoff unstable.
  6. Stuff+ is useful but incomplete. Stuff+ measures physical pitch characteristics and captures a stable part of pitch quality, but it does not directly represent every path to a strikeout, including location, called strikes, count management, and batter interaction. Location+ or Pitching+ could add process information, but they should be tested for incremental rather than assumed value.

Why swinging-strike rate is the first external-data candidate¶

Swinging-strike rate (SwStr%) is swinging strikes divided by total pitches. Whiff% is swinging strikes divided by swings. SwStr% is the preferred first candidate because its total-pitch denominator combines how often a pitcher induces swings with how often those swings miss; it therefore measures missed bats produced per pitch, a process closely connected to strikeout creation. Whiff% isolates bat-missing ability conditional on a swing, but it can overlook whether the pitcher induces enough swings for those misses to accumulate. Neither measure captures called strikes or the full process of reaching and finishing two-strike counts.

A proper SwStr% test would add prior-year, recency- and pitch-weighted, change, and missingness features using only pre-target-season data. The feature design would be selected on 2023 and evaluated once on 2024. It should be retained only if it produces a meaningful, consistent improvement over Ridge because prior K% and Stuff+ may already contain much of the same information. External data are not added to the current scope: the clean, reproducible core model is stronger than a late feature whose collection and player-season joins have not been fully validated. SwStr% is the first extension to test, followed by Whiff%, Pitching+/Location+, and then BB%.

Definitions and context: https://library.fangraphs.com/pitching/plate-discipline-o-swing-z-swing-etc/ and https://library.fangraphs.com/pitching/stuff-location-and-pitching-primer/

Reproducibility and citations¶

Run all cells from top to bottom with the project root or notebooks/ as the working directory. The notebook reads data/k_2026.csv, verifies the cutoff and feature integrity, reconstructs every historical fold, refits the selected model, and writes outputs/k_2025_predictions.csv. Package versions are recorded in environment.yml.
